title: Arguing for Sodom (Genesis 18:16–33)
hook: Abraham bargains with God from fifty righteous people down to ten

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sarah laughs, and a baby named he laughs. Your line was nothing is too hard. Did you laugh at something impossible, and take a step? Day forty-five.

The guests get up to go, and they look down toward Sodom. Abraham walks them out, the way you walk a friend to the car. And God decides to tell him something. The outcry from Sodom and its sister city Gomorrah is great, God says, and their sin very heavy. I'm going down to see. The two travelers head off toward the city. And the Torah says Abraham stays, still standing before God. Now, Sodom is not Abraham's town. These aren't his people, though his nephew Lot lives there. He could shrug. Instead, he steps closer and opens his mouth. What follows is a man haggling with God, like a customer in a market, over the lives of strangers.
screen: `THE OUTCRY OF SODOM.` → `ABRAHAM STAYS, STANDING.` → `HE STEPS CLOSER.`

segments.voice: In the old JPS translation, Abraham says: "Wilt Thou indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" What if there are fifty good people in the city? Will you destroy it, and not spare it for their sake? Far be it from you. And then the line at the heart of the scene: "shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" God agrees: for fifty, I'll spare the whole place. And Abraham keeps going. What if there are forty-five? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? Again and again he apologizes, and each time he pushes. He calls himself one "who am but dust and ashes," and in the same breath he argues with the Judge of the world. Humble and bold at once. The Tanakh comes back to it: Moses will argue with God for his people. Job will argue for himself. And Hasidic stories tell of Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, who was said to call God to account on behalf of his suffering community. In this story, arguing for mercy isn't treated as disrespect. Some readers notice that God chose to tell Abraham first, as if inviting the argument. Then Abraham stops at ten. Why ten? Rashi, the medieval commentator, points back to the flood: Noah's family was only eight, and that wasn't enough to save their world. And some teachers draw a contrast with Noah himself. When he heard the flood was coming, he built his ark and said nothing for anyone else. Abraham hears of a doomed city full of strangers, and he argues.
screen: `WILT THOU SWEEP AWAY THE RIGHTEOUS?` · `FIFTY, FORTY, THIRTY, TEN.` · `DUST AND ASHES, AND BOLD.` · `WHY STOP AT TEN?` · then, large: `SHALL NOT THE JUDGE DO JUSTLY?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who gets talked about when they're not there. A coworker whose mistakes get repeated. A relative everyone rolls their eyes at. A group of people who make an easy punchline. Picture the room where it happens. Now picture yourself saying one sentence for them. Not a speech. Just: I think there's more to it. Or: that's not fair. Notice how small it is, and whether it's hard. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Arguing for Sodom. Abraham, dust and ashes, bargaining with God from fifty good people down to ten, for a city of strangers.
Your line: argue for mercy. Today, speak up once for someone who isn't in the room. One sentence is enough. Day forty-five.

howItsDone: Jews read Abraham's argument in the Torah portion Vayera, and his question "shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" is often cited as the root of a Jewish tradition of arguing with God for mercy.

original.note: Hebrew: far be it from you. Abraham says it to God twice in one verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: Abraham bargained like a trader.
what it means: a man who calls himself dust and ashes argues with God for strangers, and God listens.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on 18:32: he stopped at ten because Noah's eight hadn't been enough to save their generation.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 18:23, 18:25 (final clause) and 18:27 ('who am but dust and ashes').
Rashi on 18:32: stopped at ten because in the generation of the flood there were eight (Noah, his sons and their wives) and they did not save it. Confirm.
Noah's silence contrasted with Abraham's argument: a common homiletic contrast (e.g. Zohar, later preachers); the script attributes it only to 'some teachers'. Confirm.
Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev (1740–1809) 'calling God to account' (the din Torah tradition): folk tradition, paraphrased. Confirm framing.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the superlative 'one of the most astonishing conversations in the Bible' and 'the line Jews have quoted to God ever since'; 'each time he apologizes' corrected to 'again and again' (he does not apologize at 45 or 40); 'runs all through Jewish tradition' narrowed to Moses and Job in the Tanakh; dropped the 'eighteenth-century' date; 'what God seems to be waiting for' reframed as what some readers notice; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel.
